sections.title: A queen's temple, a sultan's city
sections.intro_md:
On a winter morning at Palampet, sunlight hits a temple of black stone so polished that the carved dancers on its brackets look wet. A general built it in 1213 and named it, unusually, after its sculptor, Ramappa. Two hundred kilometres south-west, in the Old City of Hyderabad, the Charminar has stood since 1591 in the middle of traffic, a sultan's centrepiece for a new city of gardens and palaces.

Telangana is both. It is a dry plateau of granite and tanks where the Kakatiya kings and a woman ruler, Rudrama Devi, built for eternity, and it is the land of the Qutb Shahis and the Nizams, whose Golconda diamonds and Urdu court culture made Hyderabad famous. It is also India's youngest state, carved out of Andhra Pradesh on 2 June 2014 after a struggle that lasted, on and off, 60 years.

sections.title: Where you are
sections.intro_md:
Telangana sits in the middle of the Deccan plateau, in the south-centre of India, with no coast. Maharashtra lies to the north-west, Chhattisgarh to the north-east, Karnataka to the west and Andhra Pradesh to the south and east. Two great rivers cross it: the Godavari in the north and the Krishna along the south.

At about 112,077 km² it is India's 11th-largest state. The 2011 census counted about 3.5 crore people; the state is now estimated at about 3.85 crore. Hyderabad and its suburbs hold roughly a third of them and most of the money. The state has 33 districts, 119 Assembly seats and 17 Lok Sabha seats. Telugu is the official language and Urdu the second official language. The Indian National Congress has governed since December 2023, with A. Revanth Reddy as Chief Minister.

sections.title: The land: granite, two rivers and 46,000 tanks
sections.intro_md:
Telangana is plateau country, mostly 300 to 700 m above sea level, on some of the oldest rock in India. The granite breaks into piles of rounded boulders, which is why every fort here sits on a rock hill. Rain is modest and unreliable, about 900 mm a year, and the soils are thin red earth in the south and black cotton soil in the north.

That made water the central problem of every ruler. The Godavari and the Krishna run along the edges in deep valleys, too low to irrigate the uplands by gravity. So people stored rain in tanks for a thousand years, and the new state's two biggest programmes, Mission Kakatiya and the Kaleshwaram lift scheme, were both about water. The north, around Adilabad and the Godavari, is forested and hilly; the Nallamala hills in the south hold tigers.

spotlights.name: The Deccan boulders

where.label: Hyderabad and its outskirts, e.g. Mahendra Hills and Keesaragutta

spotlights.spot_it: Huge rounded granite boulders stacked on each other, some balanced on a point, in the middle of housing colonies.
spotlights.story_md: Hyderabad sits on some of the oldest rock in India: granite that cooled underground about 2.5 billion years ago and was slowly exposed as the softer rock around it wore away. Rain and heat split the granite along cracks, and the corners rounded off, leaving piles of boulders that look placed by hand. For centuries builders used them as foundations: Golconda fort and the Bhongir fort both grow out of granite hills. Since the 1990s the city has blasted thousands of them for apartments and roads. A citizens' group, the Society to Save Rocks, was set up in 1996 to campaign for them, and a handful of formations were later listed as natural heritage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The rock that made the forts possible is now in the way of the city.
spotlights.memory_hook: Billion-year-old rocks, balanced like someone forgot to finish a game of stones.

spotlights.name: The Godavari

where.label: Enters Telangana at Kandakurthi, Nizamabad, and leaves near Bhadrachalam

spotlights.spot_it: A wide, slow, sandy river with temple ghats on its banks: Basara in the north-west, Kaleshwaram, then Bhadrachalam in the east.
spotlights.story_md: The Godavari rises in the Western Ghats in Maharashtra, enters Telangana in Nizamabad district and crosses the whole north of the state before turning south into Andhra Pradesh. Almost everything holy in northern Telangana sits on it: the Saraswati temple at Basara, the Shiva temple at Kaleshwaram where the Pranahita joins it, and the Rama temple at Bhadrachalam. Every 12 years, when Jupiter enters Leo, millions bathe in it during the Godavari Pushkaralu. The river is also the state's biggest engineering bet: the Kaleshwaram project lifts its water uphill, stage by stage, into the dry interior.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The river that waters the north and runs the state's biggest gamble.
spotlights.memory_hook: One river, three temples, and pumps that push it uphill.

spotlights.name: The tanks: Pakhal, Laknavaram and 46,000 more
spotlights.when: Kakatiya era, 12th to 14th century; restored from 2015
spotlights.spot_it: A sheet of still water held back by a curving earth bund, with paddy fields stepping down below it.
spotlights.story_md: Telangana has few big rivers in its interior and thin rains, so for a thousand years people stored the monsoon in tanks, or cheruvulu: earth dams across shallow valleys, built in chains so that one overflows into the next. The Kakatiya kings and their generals built the grandest. Pakhal Lake, ordered in 1213 by King Ganapati Deva, is still about 30 square km of water inside a wildlife sanctuary. Laknavaram, in Mulugu, threads 13 islands with a suspension bridge. By the 2000s most village tanks were silted and breached. In 2015 the new state launched Mission Kakatiya to desilt and repair roughly 46,000 of them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Before canals and pumps, Telangana farmed with chains of man-made lakes.
spotlights.memory_hook: A state that grew rice in a dry land by building lakes in a row.

spotlights.name: Amrabad and the Nallamala tigers

where.label: Nallamala hills, Nagarkurnool and Nalgonda districts

spotlights.spot_it: Dry deciduous forest on red sandstone plateaus above the gorge of the Krishna, with Chenchu hamlets inside the reserve.
spotlights.story_md: When Andhra Pradesh was split in 2014, so was India's largest tiger reserve. The Telangana half, north of the Krishna, became the Amrabad Tiger Reserve: about 2,600 square km of the Nallamala hills, one of the biggest tiger reserves in India by area. Tigers here live at low density because the forest is dry and prey is thin. The reserve is also home to the Chenchus, hunter-gatherers whose families still collect honey from cliff faces. In 2019 a plan to explore for uranium inside the reserve set off protests across the state and was dropped. A second reserve, Kawal, guards the Godavari forests in the north.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Tigers, uranium and an indigenous people in the same hills.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half of India's biggest tiger reserve went to each state in the divorce.

spotlights.name: Palapitta, the Indian roller
spotlights.spot_it: A thickset bird on a wire that looks dull brown until it flies and flashes two shades of electric blue.
spotlights.story_md: The state bird, the Indian roller, is called palapitta in Telugu. It sits on telephone wires and dead branches, drops onto insects, and in the breeding season tumbles through the air, which is where the English name comes from. In Telangana it carries a festival job. On Vijayadashami, the last day of Dasara, families go out to spot a palapitta, because seeing one is taken as a sign of good luck for the year, linked to a story that the Pandavas saw one before their victory. On the same day people exchange leaves of the jammi tree, Prosopis cineraria, the state tree, calling them bangaram: gold.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Symbols chosen in 2014 were picked from village customs, not from zoos.
spotlights.memory_hook: On Dasara the gold is a leaf and the luck is a blue bird.

sections.title: People by numbers
sections.intro_md:
The 2011 census, the last one taken, counted about 3.5 crore people in what is now Telangana. About 39% lived in towns then, far above the national average, because Hyderabad pulls in migrants from every district and from across India. Estimates for 2025 put the urban share near half.

The averages hide two Telanganas. Hyderabad district had literacy of 83% in 2011; Jogulamba Gadwal had under 50%. Average income in 2025-26 was about ₹4.19 lakh a person, nearly twice the Indian figure, but most of it is earned in and around the capital. Muslims are about 12.7% of the state and far more in the Old City. Scheduled Tribes, mainly Lambadas, Koyas and Gonds, are about a tenth of the population, concentrated in the north and east.

sections.title: Deep history: monks, Kakatiyas and a queen
sections.intro_md:
Telangana's written history starts with the Satavahanas, who ruled the Deccan from around the 2nd century BCE, and with Buddhist monks who built stupas along the Krishna valley. Kotilingala, on the Godavari, has yielded some of the earliest Satavahana coins.

After centuries under Chalukya and Rashtrakuta overlords, a family of local chiefs, the Kakatiyas, made themselves independent in the 1160s and ruled from Orugallu, today's Warangal. For about 160 years they built tanks to farm a dry land and temples of a distinctive style: star-shaped platforms, black polished basalt and dolerite, bracket figures of dancers. Their most famous ruler was a woman. Their end, in 1323, came from Delhi, and the centre of power moved west toward Golconda.

data.name: Ikshvakus
data.note: approximate; Buddhist stupas on the Krishna

spotlights.name: Phanigiri and Buddhist Telangana
spotlights.when: About 3rd century BCE to 4th century CE
spotlights.spot_it: Brick foundations of a round stupa and monastery on a hilltop, with carved limestone panels and pillars inscribed in Brahmi.
spotlights.story_md: Long before temples and minarets, Telangana was Buddhist country. Along the Krishna and its tributaries, monks built stupas and monasteries under the Satavahanas and then the Ikshvakus, roughly from the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE. Phanigiri, a hill named for its hooded-snake shape, is one of the richest finds: excavations from the 2000s turned up a stupa, prayer halls, carved panels telling the Buddha's life, a gateway in pieces and Brahmi inscriptions. Similar sites dot the state, at Nelakondapalli, Kondapur and Dhulikatta. The giant Buddha in Hussain Sagar, set up in 1992, is a deliberate nod to this past.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Telangana's oldest monuments are Buddhist, not Hindu or Islamic.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before the temple and the mosque, the stupa.

spotlights.name: The Kakatiyas of Orugallu
spotlights.spot_it: Four carved stone gateways, the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, standing in an open field inside a ruined ring of walls.
spotlights.story_md: The Kakatiyas began as local chiefs and by the 13th century ruled most of the Telugu-speaking land from Orugallu, today's Warangal, a city inside three rings of walls: earth, stone and a moat. They are remembered for three things: tanks, temples and a queen. Their capital fell in 1323 to the army of the Delhi Sultanate under Ulugh Khan, the future Muhammad bin Tughluq; King Prataparudra was captured and is said to have died on the way to Delhi. The ornamental gateways of the fort survived, and one of them stands with the Charminar on the state emblem adopted in 2014.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first great Telugu kingdom was a Telangana kingdom.
spotlights.memory_hook: A gate with no wall left around it, now on every government letterhead.

spotlights.name: Rudrama Devi
spotlights.spot_it: Statues show a woman on horseback with a raised sword, often in front of the Warangal fort gateways.
spotlights.story_md: King Ganapati Deva had no son, so he named his daughter Rudrama his heir and, by most accounts, had her raised and titled as a prince, Rudradeva. She ruled for about a quarter of a century, put down rebellious nobles, fought off the Yadavas of Devagiri and finished the stone fort of Warangal. Marco Polo, passing the Telugu coast around 1292, described a kingdom ruled for 40 years by a wise widowed queen, which historians usually take to be her realm. An inscription found in 1994 suggests she died in battle around 1289. Her grandson Prataparudra succeeded her.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the very few women to rule a major Indian kingdom in her own name.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen crowned as a king, and noticed by Marco Polo.

spotlights.name: Ramappa Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A star-shaped temple on a high platform, carved from dark stone, with slender dancing women as brackets under the eaves.
spotlights.story_md: Recherla Rudra, a general of Ganapati Deva, started this Shiva temple in 1213 and it took about 40 years. It is called after its sculptor, Ramappa, and is often said to be the only major temple in India named for its maker rather than its god. The bracket figures, called madanikas, show dancers, a drummer and a snake charmer in black dolerite polished like metal. The tower is built of bricks light enough, it is claimed, to float, and the foundation sits on a box of sand meant to cushion earthquakes. It has stood through 800 years in a seismic zone. UNESCO inscribed it on 25 July 2021, Telangana's first World Heritage Site.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that the Kakatiyas were among the best builders of medieval India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A temple named after the man who carved it, standing on a sandbox.

spotlights.name: Thousand Pillar Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A low star-shaped temple of grey basalt with three shrines and a hall crowded with carved pillars, a black stone Nandi in front.
spotlights.story_md: Rudradeva, the king who made the Kakatiyas independent, built this temple in 1163 as a trikutalaya, a temple with three shrines, to Shiva, Vishnu and Surya. Its pillared hall gives it the popular name. Nobody needs to count: the thousand is a manner of speaking for a great many. After its foundation subsided, the Archaeological Survey of India took the hall apart in 2006 to rebuild it on a new base, a job that dragged on for well over a decade. The monolithic Nandi at the entrance, polished black, is one of the best-loved sculptures in the state.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The temple that marks the start of the Kakatiya style.
spotlights.memory_hook: A thousand pillars that nobody actually counted.

sections.title: Golconda: diamonds, a fort and a new city
sections.intro_md:
In 1518 a Turkmen governor of the Bahmani sultanate, Sultan Quli, declared himself independent at Golconda and founded the Qutb Shahi dynasty. His family ruled for 169 years. They were Shia Muslims of Persian culture who wrote poetry in Telugu and Dakhini as well as Persian, employed Telugu Brahmin ministers, and grew rich on diamonds, cotton cloth and the port of Machilipatnam.

In 1591 Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded Hyderabad on the Musi, with the Charminar at its heart. European travellers described a city of gardens, markets and diamond traders. It ended in 1687, when Aurangzeb took Golconda after an eight-month siege. The Qutb Shahis left the city, a garden of domed royal tombs below the fort, its Persian-Telugu court style, the Muharram processions that still run through the Old City and its villages, and a word in English for a mine of wealth.

visual.title: Ramappa or the Qutb Shahi Tombs?

spotlights.name: Golconda Fort
spotlights.when: Kakatiya mud fort; Qutb Shahi capital 1518 to 1687
spotlights.spot_it: Grey granite walls wrapping a boulder hill, with a pavilion, the Baradari, on the summit about 120 m above the plain.
spotlights.story_md: The name is usually explained as Golla Konda, shepherd's hill. A Kakatiya mud fort stood here first; the Bahmani sultans took it, and in 1518 their governor Sultan Quli declared himself independent and founded the Qutb Shahi dynasty. His successors rebuilt it in granite, with eight gates and about 10 km of outer walls. Guides at the entrance dome still clap their hands to show that the sound carries up to the summit pavilion, an alarm system that is more legend than proven. In 1687 Aurangzeb besieged it for about eight months. It fell only when a bribed officer opened a gate at night.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The fort that guarded the world's diamond trade.
spotlights.memory_hook: Clap at the gate and the king hears it on the hilltop, or so the guide says.

spotlights.name: Golconda diamonds

where.label: Mined along the Krishna, traded at Golconda

spotlights.spot_it: Stones described as type IIa: almost no nitrogen, so they look like still water. In English 'a Golconda' came to mean a mine of riches.
spotlights.story_md: Until diamonds were found in Brazil in the 1720s, almost every diamond in the world came from India, and most of the famous ones were sold at Golconda. They were dug from gravel pits along the Krishna, at Kollur and other mines now mostly in Andhra Pradesh, where visitors in 1621 reported 20,000 to 30,000 workers. The king kept every stone over about 10 carats. The Koh-i-Noor, the Hope Diamond (once the Tavernier Blue, bought by the French traveller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier in the 1660s), the Regent and the Darya-i-Noor are all linked to these mines. The word Golconda entered English for any source of fabulous wealth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The reason Hyderabad was rich before it had a single factory.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Koh-i-Noor and the Hope passed through one market town near Hyderabad.

spotlights.name: Charminar
spotlights.spot_it: A square arch with four slender minarets about 56 m tall, standing in the middle of a traffic junction in the old city.
spotlights.story_md: In 1591 Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah moved his court out of crowded Golconda and laid out a new city on the south bank of the Musi. At its centre he built the Charminar, four minarets on a square of four arches, with a small mosque on the top floor. The usual story is that it marks the end of a plague, though that is tradition rather than record. A legend says the city was first named Bhagyanagar after a dancer, Bhagmati, whom the sultan loved; historians treat it as a legend. The Charminar sits on the state emblem and on cigarette packets, biscuit tins and police badges.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The symbol of the city and of the Qutb Shahi idea of Hyderabad.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four minarets, four arches, four roads, and a mosque upstairs.

spotlights.name: Bhakta Ramadasu

where.label: Bhadrachalam, and a cell in Golconda fort

spotlights.spot_it: In Golconda fort a small dark cell holds rough carvings of Rama, Lakshmana and Hanuman, said to be his.
spotlights.story_md: Kancherla Gopanna was a tax officer for Abul Hasan Tana Shah, the last Qutb Shahi sultan, in charge of Bhadrachalam. He spent the revenue on rebuilding the Rama temple there. The sultan had him jailed in Golconda for 12 years. The story says Rama and Lakshmana appeared before the sultan disguised as servants and paid the debt in gold coins, after which Gopanna was freed and Tana Shah endowed the temple. As Ramadasu he composed devotional songs in Telugu still sung in Carnatic concerts. The custom of the state sending pearls and silk to Bhadrachalam for the Rama Navami wedding is traced back to Tana Shah.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Hindu poet, a Muslim sultan and a temple tradition that survived both.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tax officer who spent the taxes on God and did 12 years for it.

sections.title: The Nizams: the richest man in the world
sections.intro_md:
In 1724 Asaf Jah I, the Mughal governor of the Deccan, made himself effectively independent with the title Nizam-ul-Mulk. Seven Nizams ruled from Hyderabad until 1948. From 1798 they were allies of the British, gave up territory and kept their throne. Hyderabad became the largest princely state in India, about 214,000 km², with a mostly Telugu, Marathi and Kannada-speaking Hindu population under a Muslim, Urdu-speaking court.

The last two Nizams built modern Hyderabad: railways, the High Court, Osmania hospital and university, reservoirs after the great flood of 1908, its own currency and post. The countryside paid for it, through landlords who ran villages with forced labour. That split, palace splendour and rural hunger, explains much of what came next.

data.label: Area
data.note: larger than England and Scotland together

spotlights.name: Mir Osman Ali Khan, the last Nizam
spotlights.spot_it: Photos show a slight man in a long sherwani and a fez-like cap, usually looking more like a clerk than an emperor.
spotlights.story_md: The seventh Nizam ruled Hyderabad State, bigger than England and Scotland together, from 1911. On 22 February 1937 Time magazine put him on its cover as the richest man in the world, with estimates of about US$2 billion in the 1940s. He used the 185-carat Jacob Diamond as a paperweight, but was famous for thrift: cheap cigarettes, an old cap, socks he was said to darn himself. He also funded Osmania University, the Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar reservoirs built after the 1908 Musi flood, and gifts to Banaras Hindu University and Aligarh. When he died in 1967, about a million people followed the funeral.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The richest man on earth ran a state that most of its people experienced as feudal.
spotlights.memory_hook: A diamond the size of a lemon, holding down his papers.

spotlights.name: Osmania University
spotlights.spot_it: The Arts College: a granite facade with a towering central arch, part Indo-Saracenic, part Kakatiya, finished in 1939.
spotlights.story_md: In 1918 the Nizam founded Osmania University by royal decree, the first university in India to teach in an Indian language, Urdu, at every level. To make it work, a translation bureau, the Dar-ul-Tarjuma, turned thousands of textbooks in medicine, law and engineering into Urdu. The Arts College building, opened in 1939, is the campus landmark. Later the university became the furnace of Telangana politics: students led the agitation of 1969 and filled the campus again from 2009 to 2014. Telugu, English and other languages replaced Urdu as teaching languages after 1948.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that modern science could be taught in an Indian language, a century ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: A university that translated science into Urdu, then made a state.

spotlights.name: Salar Jung Museum

where.label: South bank of the Musi, Hyderabad

spotlights.when: Opened 1951; collection of Salar Jung III
spotlights.spot_it: A crescent-shaped museum by the river, and inside it a crowd around a marble woman whose face shows through a marble veil.
spotlights.story_md: Mir Yousuf Ali Khan, Salar Jung III, was prime minister of Hyderabad for two years and then spent his life and fortune collecting: jade, carpets, clocks, manuscripts, European paintings and furniture, Indian miniatures. After he died unmarried in 1949 the collection became a national museum. Two pieces are famous. The Veiled Rebecca by Giovanni Maria Benzoni, 1876, a marble figure whose face shows through a carved veil, was bought in Rome in 1876 by his grandfather, Salar Jung I. A 19th-century English musical clock has a little figure that comes out to strike the hour, and crowds gather for it at noon.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of India's three national museums, built from one man's shopping.
spotlights.memory_hook: A marble face behind a marble veil, and a crowd waiting for a clock.

sections.title: Revolt, annexation and the long road to 2014
sections.intro_md:
Modern Telangana was made by three struggles. The first, from 1946, was a peasant revolt against landlords and the Nizam's rule. The second, in 1948, was India's military takeover of Hyderabad State and the killings that followed it. The third ran from 1956 to 2014: the fight to undo the merger of Telangana with Andhra.

In 1956 the Telugu-speaking districts of Hyderabad State were joined with Andhra State to form Andhra Pradesh, with promises of protection for Telangana's jobs and budgets. Many in Telangana came to believe those promises were broken, and that water, jobs and respect went to the richer coastal districts. The demand for a separate state erupted in 1969, went quiet, and came back from 2001 until Parliament passed the bill in February 2014.

spotlights.name: The Telangana armed struggle
spotlights.spot_it: Statues of a woman in a plain sari with a sickle, Chakali Ilamma, stand in towns across the state.
spotlights.story_md: Under the Nizam, rural Telangana was run by landlords called doras and deshmukhs, who also served as village officials and moneylenders. Peasants owed them vetti, unpaid forced labour. On 4 July 1946 a landlord's men fired on a procession at Kadavendi in Warangal and killed Doddi Komarayya, a local organiser; that shot started an armed revolt led by communists through the Andhra Mahasabha. At its height in 1948 the rebels ran about 4,000 villages as communes and handed land to the tillers. A washerwoman, Chakali Ilamma, who refused to give up her land to a deshmukh, became its symbol. The Indian Army crushed the communes after 1948; the Communist Party called off the fight in 1951.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The land reforms of later decades started here.
spotlights.memory_hook: A washerwoman told the landlord no, and a revolt grew around her.

spotlights.name: Operation Polo
spotlights.spot_it: Black-and-white photos of Indian Army tanks rolling past crowds, and of a Hyderabad general handing over his surrender.
spotlights.story_md: In 1947 the Nizam refused to join India or Pakistan and wanted Hyderabad to stay independent. Inside the state a militia, the Razakars, led by Qasim Razvi, terrorised Hindu villages and opponents. On 13 September 1948 the Indian Army moved in, in an operation officially called a police action. The Nizam's forces gave up within about four days, and on 18 September Major General El Edroos surrendered to Major General J. N. Chaudhuri. Official figures put the Indian Army's dead at fewer than 10. The killing of civilians that followed was far worse: a government inquiry, the Sunderlal Committee, estimated 30,000 to 40,000 deaths, and kept its report secret until 2013.
spotlights.why_it_matters: How a princely state the size of a country joined India in five days.
spotlights.memory_hook: A police action with tanks.

spotlights.name: The 1969 Jai Telangana agitation

where.label: Osmania University and Gun Park, Hyderabad

spotlights.spot_it: A white pillar memorial at Gun Park, opposite the old Assembly, where every Telangana protest still begins or ends.
spotlights.story_md: When Andhra Pradesh was formed in 1956, Telangana leaders were given promises, the Gentlemen's Agreement, about jobs, education and spending in the region. By the late 1960s many in Telangana felt those promises had been broken, especially the mulki rules that reserved local jobs for locals. In 1969 students at Osmania University started an agitation for a separate state. It spread across the region and police firings killed many people; the memorial at Gun Park is usually said to honour 369 of them. A new party, the Telangana Praja Samithi, swept the region's seats in 1971, then merged into the Congress. The demand went quiet for 30 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first time Telangana asked to leave, and the first martyrs' list.
spotlights.memory_hook: A university started a movement that waited 45 years to win.

spotlights.name: The road to 2 June 2014
spotlights.spot_it: The Telangana Martyrs Memorial on the Tank Bund: a steel lamp-shaped building that glows gold at night, opened in 2023.
spotlights.story_md: In April 2001 K. Chandrashekar Rao left the Telugu Desam Party and founded the Telangana Rashtra Samithi with one demand. On 29 November 2009 he began a fast unto death; on 9 December the Union Home Minister announced that the process to form Telangana would begin, then stepped back two weeks later after protests in Andhra. What followed was four years of strikes and marches: a 42-day general strike in 2011, the Million March, resignations of MLAs and MPs, and the suicides of young people. The Andhra Pradesh Assembly rejected the bill in a voice vote in about 15 seconds; Parliament passed it in February 2014. Telangana was born on 2 June 2014, with Rao as its first Chief Minister.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's newest large state, made by a 13-year campaign.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fast in 2009, a state in 2014.

sections.title: Languages: Telangana Telugu, Dakhini, Lambadi
sections.intro_md:
Three quarters of Telangana speaks Telugu at home, but not the Telugu of old textbooks. Telangana Telugu carries hundreds of Urdu and Persian words from four centuries of Deccan sultanates and Nizams, and its own sounds and grammar. For decades films used it for villains and comic servants. Since statehood it has become a badge of pride, and films and songs in it now travel across India.

Urdu is the second official language and the first language of about one person in eight, most in Hyderabad. Hyderabad's own Urdu, Dakhini, is older than the Urdu of Delhi as a literary language. Then come tribal languages: Lambadi, Gondi and Koya. Many Hyderabadis switch between Telugu, Dakhini, Hindi and English in a single sentence.

spotlights.name: Dakhini, Hyderabad's Urdu

where.label: Hyderabad, and the old Deccan sultanates

spotlights.spot_it: Listen for hau (yes), nakko (no), kaiku (why) and the all-purpose 'kya bolte' in any Old City conversation.
spotlights.story_md: Dakhini is the Urdu of the Deccan, born when soldiers and settlers from north India came south with the Delhi Sultanate in the 14th century and mixed their speech with Telugu, Marathi and Kannada. It became a written literary language in the Deccan courts before Urdu poetry flowered in Delhi. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the founder of Hyderabad, is often called the first poet to compile a full diwan, a collected volume, in Urdu. Modern standard Urdu treats Dakhini as a dialect, and Bollywood uses it for comedy, but it is the everyday tongue of millions of Hyderabadis, Hindu and Muslim alike.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The language of the city is a 600-year-old mixture of north and south.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hau for yes, nakko for no: the founder of the city wrote poems in it.

spotlights.name: Kaloji Narayana Rao and Telangana Telugu
spotlights.spot_it: An old man with a white beard and thick glasses, in a plain kurta: the face on Telangana's language day posters.
spotlights.story_md: For decades Telangana people heard their Telugu mocked as rough village speech next to the coastal Andhra standard used in films, textbooks and news. Kaloji Narayana Rao, a poet from Warangal who went to jail under the Nizam and spent his life defending civil liberties, wrote deliberately in the speech of ordinary Telangana people and made it a matter of pride. His birthday, 9 September, is now celebrated as Telangana Language Day, and the state's health university is named after him. Since 2014 Telangana Telugu has moved from comic sidekick to film hero: dialect-heavy films from Hyderabad now sell all over India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Language was at the heart of the statehood fight.
spotlights.memory_hook: The poet who made village Telugu respectable.

spotlights.name: The Lambadas (Banjaras)

where.label: Tandas across Telangana, many in Mahabubabad, Khammam and Nalgonda

spotlights.spot_it: Women in mirror-work skirts and backless blouses, with heavy silver jewellery and bone or ivory-coloured bangles to the elbow.
spotlights.story_md: Lambadi, or Gor Boli, was the mother tongue of about 5.5% of people in Telangana in 2011, more than Hindi. The Lambadas, also called Banjaras or Sugalis, descend from caravan traders who carried grain and salt across India for armies and markets until railways ended the trade. They now live in hamlets called tandas, and in 2018 the state turned hundreds of tandas into gram panchayats of their own. They are a Scheduled Tribe in Telangana, the largest one, which has caused friction with older forest tribes such as the Gonds and Koyas over reserved jobs. The Teej festival in August brings tandas together.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Telangana's largest tribal community, with a language most people never notice.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mirror-work, silver and a caravan language still spoken in 2026.

sections.title: Faith: Rama's river, a rebuilt hill, a famine church
sections.intro_md:
About 85% of Telangana is Hindu, 12.7% Muslim and 1.3% Christian. Village faith centres on goddesses: Pochamma, Maisamma, Yellamma, the Mahakali of Bonalu. Big pilgrim temples sit on the Godavari and on hills, and the new state used temples as symbols, rebuilding Yadagirigutta in stone and sending the state's gifts to Bhadrachalam.

Islam came with the Bahmanis and Qutb Shahis. The Mecca Masjid beside the Charminar, begun in 1617, is one of the largest mosques in India. Christianity grew among Dalit and poor rural communities through Methodist, Anglican and Catholic missions, whose cathedral at Medak rose out of a famine. And the line between faiths is not always sharp: Hindus keep Muharram in the villages, and a sultan's state sent pearls to Rama.

spotlights.name: Bhadrachalam

where.label: Bhadradri Kothagudem district, on the Godavari

spotlights.spot_it: A white gopuram above the Godavari at the eastern edge of the state, with steps down to bathing ghats.
spotlights.story_md: The temple of Sita and Rama at Bhadrachalam is the most important Rama shrine in the Telugu lands. Its rebuilding by Kancherla Gopanna, Bhakta Ramadasu, cost him 12 years in Golconda's jail. Every year on Sri Rama Navami the divine wedding, Sita Rama Kalyanam, is performed here, and the state government sends silk clothes and pearls, the talambralu, a custom traced back to the Qutb Shahi sultan Tana Shah. The nearby Parnasala is where, in local tradition, Ravana carried Sita off. In 2014 the Godavari villages around Bhadrachalam were split: the temple town stayed in Telangana, several surrounding mandals went to Andhra Pradesh.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Rama wedding that a Muslim dynasty helped pay for, every year since the 1680s.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pearls for Sita, from the government, every spring.

spotlights.name: Medak Cathedral
spotlights.spot_it: A grey stone Gothic church with a 53 m bell tower rising out of paddy fields in a small town.
spotlights.story_md: Charles Walker Posnett, a British Methodist missionary, arrived in Medak in 1895. During a famine he started building a great church and paid the hungry in grain for their work, so the cathedral was built as famine relief. It was consecrated on Christmas Day 1924. Its stained-glass windows, made in England, show the Ascension and the Nativity; its floor tiles came from Britain and the stone was quarried locally. It is the seat of the Diocese of Medak of the Church of South India, among the largest dioceses in that church. At Christmas tens of thousands of visitors of every faith come.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A cathedral built by famine workers, now one of the largest churches in Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Grain for stone: the church a famine built.

spotlights.name: Basara and the first letters

where.label: Basara, Nirmal district, on the Godavari

spotlights.when: Year round, especially on Vasant Panchami
spotlights.spot_it: Parents sit a small child before a priest who guides the child's finger to trace letters in a plate of rice.
spotlights.story_md: The Gnana Saraswati temple at Basara, where the Godavari enters Telangana, is one of very few major temples in South India dedicated to Saraswati, goddess of learning. Families bring children of two or three for aksharabhyasam, the first writing of letters: the priest holds the child's finger and writes Om and the first letter of the Telugu alphabet in rice or on a slate. On Vasant Panchami and during Navaratri the queues run for hours. Tradition says the sage Vyasa meditated here and shaped the goddess's image from sand.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Education is a sacred act in Telangana families, and this is where it begins.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your first letter, written in rice, at the river's door.

sections.title: Festivals: flowers, pots and the world's biggest tribal fair
sections.intro_md:
Telangana's festivals are loud, public and led by women and tribal priests more than by Brahmin temples. Two became symbols of the statehood movement: Bathukamma, the flower festival of autumn, and Bonalu, the summer offering to the goddess. Both are now official state festivals with public holidays and government budgets.

The forests of the north and east add their own: the Koya jatara of Medaram, the Raj Gond Nagoba jatara at Keslapur and the Dandari dances around Diwali. In Hyderabad, Ganesh Chaturthi ends with tens of thousands of idols immersed in Hussain Sagar, led by the giant Ganesha of Khairatabad. On Vijayadashami people hunt the sky for a palapitta and exchange jammi leaves as gold.

data.name: Sankranti, with sakinalu; Medaram in alternate years (Jan or Feb)
Nagoba Jatara at Keslapur (Jan or Feb)
Sri Rama Navami wedding at Bhadrachalam (March or April)
Ganesh immersion in Hussain Sagar (Aug or Sep)
Bathukamma and Dasara: palapitta and jammi leaves (Sep or Oct)
Dandari and Gusadi in Adilabad, around Diwali

spotlights.name: Bathukamma

where.label: Every village and city in Telangana

spotlights.when: Nine days ending on Durgashtami, September or October
spotlights.spot_it: Cone-shaped towers of flowers in rings of yellow, pink and purple, and circles of women clapping and singing around them.
spotlights.story_md: Bathukamma means mother goddess, come alive. For nine days before Dasara, women stack seasonal flowers, especially yellow tangedu (the state flower, Senna auriculata) and gunugu, in concentric rings on a plate into a temple-shaped tower, with a little turmeric Gauramma on top. In the evening they place them in the middle of the street and dance in a circle, clapping and singing songs that pass on family stories, grief and gossip. On the last day, Saddula Bathukamma, the towers are floated in tanks and lakes. The festival became a flag of the statehood movement. On 29 September 2025 a Bathukamma 63 feet high, built from about seven tonnes of flowers, set a Guinness record.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The festival that turned into the symbol of a state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A temple made of flowers, built by women, sent off on the water.

spotlights.name: Bonalu

where.label: Golconda, Secunderabad, Lal Darwaza and every basti of Hyderabad

spotlights.spot_it: Women carrying decorated brass or clay pots on their heads, lamps burning on the lids, led by a turmeric-smeared man cracking a whip.
spotlights.story_md: Bonam means a meal: rice cooked with milk and jaggery in a new pot, carried on a woman's head to the goddess Mahakali or one of her village forms. The festival runs through the month of Ashadha, starting at Golconda and moving to the Ujjaini Mahankali temple in Secunderabad and the Lal Darwaza temple in the Old City. Local tradition links the Secunderabad celebration to a vow made by soldiers in 1813 during a cholera outbreak. The procession is led by Pothuraju, the goddess's brother, in a red cloth and ankle bells. In the rangam ritual a woman possessed by the goddess predicts the year. It became a state festival in 2014.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hyderabad's own festival, older than the city's bridges.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pot of sweet rice, a lamp on the lid, and a whip to clear the road.

spotlights.name: Medaram Jatara
spotlights.when: Every two years in January or February; last held 28 to 31 January 2026
spotlights.spot_it: A sea of people in a forest clearing, carrying jaggery in sacks, and Koya priests bringing two goddesses in on bamboo poles.
spotlights.story_md: Every two years, in January or February, the forest village of Medaram fills with millions of people for four days. They come for Sammakka and her daughter Saralamma, Koya tribal women who, in the story, fought a Kakatiya army that demanded tax in a year of drought; the death of Sammakka's son Jampanna turned the local stream red, and it is still called Jampanna Vagu. The goddesses are not idols but objects brought from the forest by Koya priests, who run every ritual. Devotees offer bangaram, gold, which here means jaggery, often their own body weight in it. In 1955 about 2,000 people came. For the 2026 jatara, held 28 to 31 January, estimates ran from about 80 lakh to more than 1.6 crore. It is often called the biggest tribal festival in the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A tribal festival that has grown into one of India's largest gatherings.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your own weight in jaggery, for a goddess who fought the king's tax men.

spotlights.name: Peerla Panduga

where.label: Villages across Telangana; Bibi ka Alam procession in Hyderabad

spotlights.spot_it: In a village, Hindu men carry metal hand-shaped standards, the peerlu, decorated with flowers, and walk through a pit of embers.
spotlights.story_md: Muharram is a month of mourning for Shia Muslims, recalling the death of Imam Hussain at Karbala in 680. In Hyderabad the Bibi ka Alam, a standard said to hold a relic of the Prophet's daughter Fatima, is carried on an elephant through the Old City on the 10th day. In Telangana villages the same days have become Peerla Panduga, a festival in which Hindus, often more than Muslims, raise the peerlu, the metal standards, in a shrine, sing laments, and walk on fire. Folklorists see it as a legacy of four centuries of Shia rule under the Qutb Shahis.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The clearest example of Telangana's shared Hindu and Muslim religious life.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Shia mourning that Hindu villagers walk on fire for.

sections.title: Dance, song, scrolls and film
sections.intro_md:
Telangana's performing arts run on two tracks. One is courtly and reconstructed: Perini, the Kakatiya warrior dance rebuilt in the 20th century from a 13th-century text and temple carvings. The other is the living folk of the villages and forests: Gond Gusadi dancers in peacock crowns, oggu katha drummers who sing the tales of Mallanna, the dappu drum of Dalit musicians, and the storytellers whose painted Cheriyal scrolls ran 40 feet.

The folk track became political. Ballads by Gaddar, Goreti Venkanna and many others carried the statehood movement, and dhoom dhaam cultural nights filled every rally. Hyderabad is also home to the Telugu film industry, whose 2022 film RRR took a Telangana tribal hero to the Oscars stage.

rows.gusadi: Young Raj Gond men in a village troupe

rows.perini: Bare chest, dhoti, ankle bells, fierce Shiva poses
rows.gusadi: Huge peacock-feather crown, ash, beads, goatskin

rows.perini: Rebuilt by Nataraja Ramakrishna from text and carvings
rows.gusadi: Never lost; master Kanaka Raju got the Padma Shri in 2021

spotlights.name: Perini Sivatandavam
spotlights.spot_it: Bare-chested men in dhotis leaping and stamping to loud drums, arms stiff like swords, in a fierce dance to Shiva.
spotlights.story_md: Perini was the warriors' dance of the Kakatiyas, performed before battle to call Shiva's fury into the soldiers' bodies. It is described in the Nritta Ratnavali, a treatise on dance written in the 1250s by Jayapa Senani, a Kakatiya commander of elephants who was also a dance theorist. After Warangal fell in 1323 the dance vanished. In the 20th century the dancer and scholar Nataraja Ramakrishna rebuilt it from the text and from the dancing figures carved at Ramappa. It is now the state's signature dance at official events, performed mostly by men with heavy drumming.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A dance rebuilt from a book and a temple wall.
spotlights.memory_hook: Soldiers dancing themselves into a rage for Shiva.

spotlights.name: Gusadi

where.label: Raj Gond villages of Adilabad and Kumram Bheem Asifabad

spotlights.spot_it: Dancers in enormous headdresses of peacock feathers, faces and bodies smeared with ash or paint, ankle bells, and a deerskin.
spotlights.story_md: During Dandari, the Raj Gond festival around Diwali, troupes travel from village to village, and the Gusadi dancers lead them: young men transformed by a peacock-feather crown that can be a metre across, beads, a goatskin, ash on the body and sometimes a mask. A Gusadi is treated as a god while in costume, and people touch his feet. The dance is wild and loose, with jumps and turns to drums, flutes and horns. Kanaka Raju, a Gond master of the form, received the Padma Shri in 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The image of Gond culture that Telangana now puts on posters.
spotlights.memory_hook: For one week a year, a village boy in peacock feathers is a god.

spotlights.name: Cheriyal scroll painting
spotlights.spot_it: Long cloth scrolls in panels, figures with big eyes on bright red backgrounds, telling stories frame by frame like a comic strip.
spotlights.story_md: Cheriyal scrolls were the props of travelling storytellers. Each caste had its bards and its scroll: the toddy tappers' scroll told their origin story, the weavers' theirs, the shepherds' the tales of Mallanna. A scroll could be 40 or 50 feet long, with a panel for each episode, unrolled as the bard sang through the night. The painters, a family of Nakashi artists, use cloth coated with rice starch, tamarind seed paste and white clay, and natural colours on a red ground. With television the bards disappeared. A handful of Nakashi families now paint smaller panels, masks and dolls for buyers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Telangana's comic strip, older than comics.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 40-foot scroll was one night's show.

spotlights.name: Telugu cinema and Ramoji Film City
spotlights.spot_it: Fake palaces, a fake airport, fake streets of Mumbai and London, all on a 2,000-acre hillside east of the city.
spotlights.story_md: Telugu films moved their home from Madras to Hyderabad from the 1970s on, and the industry, often called Tollywood, is now one of India's two biggest by tickets sold. In 1996 the media owner Ramoji Rao opened Ramoji Film City on about 2,000 acres, and in 2005 Guinness recognised it as the world's largest film studio complex. Baahubali was shot there. In March 2023 RRR's Naatu Naatu, from a Hyderabad production, became the first song from an Indian film to win the Oscar for best original song.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hyderabad makes the films that the rest of India now dubs.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's biggest film set, with a fake airport and a real queue of tourists.

spotlights.name: Gaddar and the songs of the movement

where.label: Toopran, Medak and the whole state

spotlights.spot_it: A man in a black blanket and dhoti, ankle bells, a stick in hand, singing and dancing in front of a crowd of thousands.
spotlights.story_md: Gaddar was born Gummadi Vittal Rao in a Dalit family and became the most famous revolutionary balladeer in India, singing for the Naxalite left from the 1970s. His concerts used folk forms, the dappu drum and the oggu katha storytelling beat, and crowds sang his songs word for word. In 1997 unknown gunmen shot him; one bullet stayed in his spine for the rest of his life. In the 2000s he threw his voice behind the statehood movement, whose songs, from Gaddar, Goreti Venkanna and others, filled every rally. He died in August 2023. In 2025 the state renamed its film awards the Gaddar Awards.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Telangana was sung into existence as much as argued into it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bullet in his spine and a song in every mouth.

sections.title: Crafts and handloom
sections.intro_md:
Handloom is Telangana's biggest craft and its oldest export. Hand-woven cotton from the Deccan was sold through Machilipatnam to Persia, Southeast Asia and Europe under the Qutb Shahis. Today the main centres are Pochampally and the villages around it for ikat, Gadwal and Narayanpet for saris, and Siddipet for Gollabhama saris with figures of milkmaids.

Other crafts are tied to a town and often to one family network: Nirmal for painted wooden toys, Karimnagar for silver filigree, Cheriyal for scroll paintings, Adilabad for Gond brass casting, the lanes behind the Charminar for lac bangles and pearls. Many carry Geographical Indication tags. The craft economy is fragile: power looms copy ikat patterns cheaply, and in the 2000s debt drove a wave of weaver suicides in the handloom towns.

spotlights.name: Pochampally ikat
spotlights.spot_it: Sharp geometric diamonds and zigzags with slightly blurred, feathered edges, the sign that the yarn was dyed before weaving.
spotlights.story_md: In ikat the pattern is dyed into the threads before the cloth exists. Weavers tie off sections of yarn with rubber or thread, dye them, retie, dye again, then set the threads on the loom so the colours meet to form the design. A tiny misalignment gives ikat its soft, flickering edges. Pochampally weavers do it in silk and cotton, and the Telia rumal, an oiled ikat once worn by fishermen and Arab traders, is a related form. In 1999 a local weaver, Chintakindi Mallesham, invented a machine, the Laxmi ASU, to wind the yarn and spare his mother's arms; it became the subject of a 2019 film. Pochampally was named one of UNWTO's best tourism villages in 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of India's great ikats, made 50 km from HITEC City.
spotlights.memory_hook: The pattern is dyed into the thread before the cloth exists.

spotlights.name: Laad Bazaar lac bangles
spotlights.spot_it: Shops lit like jewel boxes, walls of bangles covered in coloured stones and mirrors, and a man heating lac over a small flame.
spotlights.story_md: Laad Bazaar runs west from the Charminar and is the oldest bangle market in the city; laad means lac. Lac is a resin secreted by insects on trees, the same material as shellac. Artisans heat it, colour it, roll it around a metal ring and press glass stones, beads and mirrors into it while it is soft. A set for a bride can have dozens of bangles per arm. Families in the lanes behind the bazaar have made them for generations, and the work is a big part of Hyderabadi wedding shopping.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A medieval market that never stopped trading.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bangles made from bug resin, glittering like the Nizam's jewels.

sections.title: Food: biryani in the city, jowar in the villages
sections.intro_md:
There are two cuisines in Telangana and they share a chilli. Hyderabad's is the court food of the Nizams: dum biryani, haleem, kebabs, qubani ka meetha, double ka meetha, slow-cooked and rich, drawing on Persian, Mughal, Arab and Telugu kitchens. The countryside eats sorghum and rice, sour greens such as gongura and tamarind, red chilli, sesame and peanuts, and meat on festival days.

Telangana food is hotter and more sour than coastal Andhra food, and more millet-based. Dishes to know beyond the spotlights: gongura mutton, pachi pulusu (an uncooked tamarind broth), sarva pindi, malidalu (crushed roti with jaggery for Bathukamma), and pacchi pulusu with jonna annam. Toddy, kallu, is the country drink.

spotlights.name: Hyderabadi biryani
spotlights.spot_it: Long-grain rice streaked yellow and white, with pieces of meat hidden in the layers, served with mirchi ka salan and raita.
spotlights.story_md: The proud version is kacchi gosht ki biryani: raw mutton, marinated in yoghurt, spices and fried onion, is laid at the bottom of a heavy pot, covered with part-cooked rice, sealed with dough and cooked on a slow fire, dum, so the meat and rice cook together in their own steam. Getting both done at the same moment is the cook's test. It is served with mirchi ka salan, a peanut, sesame and chilli curry, and raita. Places such as Paradise, open since 1953, turned it into a city brand, and delivery apps report biryani as India's most ordered dish, with Hyderabad among the biggest buyers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dish that Hyderabad is known for around the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Raw meat at the bottom, rice on top, and a dough seal that keeps the secret.

spotlights.name: Hyderabadi haleem

where.label: Old City and every neighbourhood during Ramzan

spotlights.spot_it: A thick, glossy brown porridge of meat and wheat, topped with fried onion, mint, lime and cashews, served from big brick ovens on the street.
spotlights.story_md: Haleem came with the Chaush, Hyderabad's Arab community from Yemen, under the sixth Nizam; it began as the Arab harees of meat and pounded wheat. Hyderabad made it its own with spices and ghee. It is cooked for up to 12 hours in a bhatti, a cauldron set in a brick and mud kiln, while men beat it with long wooden paddles until the meat disappears into the grain. In 2010 it became the first non-vegetarian dish in India to receive a GI tag. During Ramzan about 6,000 eateries sell it, and in 2014 sales were put at about ₹500 crore in a single month.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hyderabad's Ramzan economy runs on a porridge.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve hours of beating meat into wheat with a paddle.

spotlights.name: Irani chai and Osmania biscuits
spotlights.spot_it: A small glass of thick, sweet, milky tea, with a round salty-sweet biscuit dunked in it, at a marble-topped table under a slow ceiling fan.
spotlights.story_md: Irani cafes were opened by Zoroastrian and Muslim migrants from Iran, many from Yazd, who came to Hyderabad from the late 19th century. Their tea is made differently: milk is boiled down for hours until thick and sweet, the tea brewed strong separately, and the two mixed in the glass. The Osmania biscuit, salty and sweet and melting, is said to have been created for the Nizam or for Osmania hospital patients; its origin is told in several versions. Cafe Niloufer, opened in 1978, is among the busiest in the city. Hundreds of old Irani cafes have closed, but the drink is everywhere.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hyderabad's social life happens over these glasses.
spotlights.memory_hook: Milk boiled for hours, tea brewed separately, a biscuit that cannot decide if it is sweet or salty.

spotlights.name: Sakinalu
spotlights.spot_it: Flat concentric coils of rice dough, flecked with sesame and ajwain, fried golden and stacked high in a basket.
spotlights.story_md: If one snack says Telangana, it is sakinalu. Before Sankranti women soak and grind rice, mix the flour with sesame, ajwain and salt, and pipe it by hand onto a cloth in rings of three or four loops. The rings dry, then fry crisp. Making them is a social event, with neighbours working together. Mothers send big batches with their daughters after a wedding, as saare, and families send them to relatives in the Gulf and the US. Andhra and Rayalaseema have similar snacks, but the sakinalu shape and its sesame bite are Telangana's own.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The taste of a Telangana home at Sankranti.
spotlights.memory_hook: A spiral of rice that every daughter carries to her new home.

spotlights.name: Jonna rotte and sarva pindi

where.label: Dry districts of the north and west

spotlights.spot_it: A thick, pale, slightly cracked flatbread of jowar flour, slapped thin by hand, eaten with greens, peanut chutney or curry.
spotlights.story_md: Outside Hyderabad, Telangana's everyday food is not biryani but millet and rice. Jonna rotte, flatbread of sorghum (jowar), is patted thin with wet palms and baked on an iron pan, then eaten with leafy greens, red chilli chutney or pulusu. Sarva pindi is a crisp rice-flour pancake with chana dal, peanuts and green chilli, pressed into a pot with the fingers so that it has holes, then cooked with a lid. In a dry state, jowar and millets were survival food. Now they are back in Hyderabad cafes as health food.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The real food of rural Telangana, closer to Maharashtra and Karnataka than to Andhra.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bread made from the grain that survives a drought.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Telangana life is shaped by caste, land and migration. Backward Classes such as the Gouds, Gollas, Kurumas, Mudirajs and weavers make up more than half the population by the state's 2024 caste survey; Scheduled Castes are about a sixth and Scheduled Tribes about a tenth. Land conflicts with doras, the old landlord families, sit in living memory.

Many families have a son in Hyderabad, the Gulf or the US. The Gulf route from north Telangana districts such as Jagtial and Nizamabad is old and hard; the American route from Hyderabad's engineering colleges is newer and richer. Weddings are long and lavish, with turmeric ceremonies and the bride's family sending sakinalu and sweets as saare. Toddy, chicken and mutton on Sundays, and Bonalu in July mark the village week and year.

spotlights.name: Kallu: toddy and the Gouds
spotlights.spot_it: A man climbing a tall palm with a rope loop around his feet and a pot on his waist, at first light.
spotlights.story_md: Toddy, kallu, is the sap of palmyra and date palms, tapped at dawn and drunk the same day as it starts to ferment. In rural Telangana it is ordinary food and drink, served in village kallu compounds, poured at festivals and offered to village gods. Tapping is the hereditary work of the Goud community, one of the state's largest, and climbing is dangerous: falls kill and cripple tappers every year. The state government planted millions of palms on tank bunds and canal banks and in 2024 began handing out climbing safety kits. Adulterated toddy, cut with chemicals, has killed people in recent years and is a regular police story.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A drink that is also an economy and a caste identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sap at dawn, a party by noon.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
The people Telangana honours most are fighters and builders. Komaram Bheem and Chakali Ilamma stand for the poor who fought the Nizam's order. P. V. Narasimha Rao, a village boy from Karimnagar district, opened India's economy. Sarojini Naidu grew up in the Nizam's Hyderabad and carried its bazaars into English poetry.

Hyderabad also produces champions out of all proportion: badminton players from Pullela Gopichand's academy, including P. V. Sindhu and Saina Nehwal, Mithali Raj in cricket, Sania Mirza in tennis, Nikhat Zareen in boxing. Satya Nadella, Microsoft's chief since 2014, went to school in Begumpet. Others worth knowing: Professor Jayashankar, the ideologue of statehood; K. Chandrashekar Rao, its political leader; and the poet Dasarathi Krishnamacharyulu, who wrote verse on prison walls under the Nizam.

spotlights.name: P. V. Narasimha Rao
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy-lidded, pouting man with white hair in a dhoti or bandhgala, almost never smiling for the camera.
spotlights.story_md: Born in a village in Telangana in 1921, P. V. Narasimha Rao fought in the anti-Nizam movement as a young man, became Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh in 1971 and pushed land reform. He spoke about ten languages and wrote a novel. In June 1991, with India close to defaulting on its debts, he became Prime Minister and, with his finance minister Manmohan Singh, opened the economy: devalued the rupee, cut licences and tariffs, invited foreign investment. The reforms reshaped India. The demolition of the Babri Masjid in 1992 happened on his watch and stains his record. In 2024 he was awarded the Bharat Ratna.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Telangana man who opened India's economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten languages, and one decision in 1991 that changed all of them.

spotlights.name: Sarojini Naidu

where.label: Hyderabad; her home, the Golden Threshold

spotlights.spot_it: A round-faced woman with large eyes, hair parted in the middle, in a draped sari, often beside Gandhi.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Hyderabad in 1879 to a Bengali scientist father who ran the Nizam's college, Sarojini Chattopadhyay was a child prodigy who went to study in London on a scholarship from the Nizam. Her English poems, about Hyderabad bazaars, bangle sellers and palanquin bearers, made her famous as the Nightingale of India. She married a doctor from outside her caste, joined Gandhi, led the 1930 Dharasana salt raid after Gandhi's arrest, and became the first Indian woman to preside over the Indian National Congress, in 1925, and the first woman governor of an Indian state in 1947. Her birthday, 13 February, is National Women's Day in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hyderabad gave India its first woman Congress president and governor.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Nightingale of India wrote about the bangle sellers of Hyderabad.

spotlights.name: Komaram Bheem
spotlights.spot_it: Statues of a Gond man with a turban, a bow or a gun, and the slogan Jal, Jangal, Zameen beneath him.
spotlights.story_md: Komaram Bheem was a Gond leader who fought the Nizam's forest officials and the landlords and moneylenders who took Gond land. From the late 1930s he organised Gond villages around Jodeghat and Babejhari to defend their land and claim the right to farm the forest, under the slogan Jal, Jangal, Zameen: water, forest, land. In 1940 the Nizam's police surrounded his group and killed him with a number of his followers. The slogan outlived him and became the motto of adivasi movements across India. His story reached a mass audience in 2022 through RRR, whose hero is very loosely based on him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Gond hero whose slogan became India's adivasi rallying cry.
spotlights.memory_hook: Water, forest, land: three words that outlived the Nizam.

spotlights.name: Mithali Raj, Sania Mirza and Nikhat Zareen
spotlights.spot_it: Three women who changed what Indian girls thought they could do: a batter, a tennis player, a boxer.
spotlights.story_md: Mithali Raj, who grew up in Secunderabad, played women's cricket for India from 1999 to 2022 and retired as the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket. Sania Mirza, from Hyderabad, became the first Indian woman to win a WTA singles title, in Hyderabad in 2005, and won six Grand Slam titles in doubles and mixed doubles, reaching world No. 1 in doubles in 2015. Nikhat Zareen, from Nizamabad, won boxing world titles in 2022 and 2023, after a girlhood in which relatives told her boxing was not for girls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hyderabad has produced more top Indian sportswomen than most countries.
spotlights.memory_hook: A batter, a racket and a pair of gloves, all from one region.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
A first trip: two days in Hyderabad for the Charminar, Laad Bazaar, Mecca Masjid, Chowmahalla, Salar Jung Museum, Golconda at sunset and the Qutb Shahi Tombs, with Irani chai at every stop. Then a day east to Warangal for the fort's gateways, the Thousand Pillar Temple, Ramappa and Laknavaram Lake. Add Pochampally on the way for ikat.

With more time: Bhadrachalam and the Godavari boat trips that run downriver into the Papikondalu gorge, Basara on the Godavari, Kuntala falls after the monsoon, the Bhongir rock fort an hour from Hyderabad, and Nagarjuna Sagar's island museum of Buddhist relics. Visit from October to February; April and May often pass 42 degrees. Respect forest rules at Amrabad, where entry is limited.

spotlights.name: Hussain Sagar and the Buddha
spotlights.spot_it: A white granite Buddha standing on a rock in the middle of a city lake, with the Tank Bund road and its statues along one side.
spotlights.story_md: Hussain Sagar was dug in 1563 under Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah, fed by a channel from the Musi, and named after Hussain Shah Wali, who oversaw the work. It still divides Hyderabad from Secunderabad. In the 1980s the state ordered an 18 m Buddha carved from a single block of white granite. During its transport onto the lake in 1990 the statue toppled into the water, and it took two years to raise it. It was set up on the Rock of Gibraltar in the lake on 12 April 1992. The Tank Bund along the east shore carries 34 bronze statues of Telugu figures. The lake is badly polluted by sewage and festival idols.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The city's living room, and one of its biggest environmental problems.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Buddha who sank, then rose again two years later.

sections.title: How the state earns
sections.intro_md:
Telangana is one of India's richest large states per person, and the money comes overwhelmingly from Hyderabad's services: software, back offices of global firms, pharmaceuticals, vaccines, real estate and trade. Services produce roughly two thirds of the state's output. The state's IT exports were about ₹2.68 lakh crore in 2023-24, from roughly 9.5 lakh tech workers.

Outside the city the economy is farming: paddy, which boomed after new irrigation, cotton, maize and chillies, with livestock and fish in the tanks. Coal from Singareni in the Godavari valley, cement and power add an older industrial layer. The new state also borrowed heavily: total debt including guarantees was put at about ₹8 lakh crore in December 2025, and the question of what the borrowing built is a political fight.

spotlights.name: HITEC City and the Financial District
spotlights.spot_it: Glass towers on bare granite, ring roads and flyovers, and the curved Cyber Towers building where it started.
spotlights.story_md: In 1998 the Andhra Pradesh government opened Cyber Towers in Madhapur, on scrubland west of the city, and invited software firms. Microsoft opened its India development centre in Hyderabad the same year. Google, Amazon, Apple, Meta and hundreds of global firms followed; Amazon built one of its largest office buildings in the world here. The area grew into HITEC City and the Financial District, and in the 2020s into a hub of global capability centres, the in-house tech and back offices of foreign companies. The state reports software exports of well over ₹2 lakh crore a year. The other side: traffic, flooding, and land prices that pushed workers far out.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The engine of the state's economy, and the reason Telangana is rich per head.
spotlights.memory_hook: Scrubland in 1997, the world's back office by 2025.

spotlights.name: Genome Valley and the vaccine makers

where.label: Turkapally and Shamirpet, north of Hyderabad

spotlights.spot_it: A low campus of labs and factories on the city's northern edge; in 2021 its product was a vial with a blue cap marked Covaxin.
spotlights.story_md: Genome Valley began in 1999 as a biotech park built with Bharat Biotech, founded by Krishna Ella. It now covers about 2,000 acres with more than 200 companies, from Indian firms such as Biological E and Bharat Biotech to multinationals including Novartis and GSK. Hyderabad's vaccine makers together produce a large share of the world's vaccine doses; officials often say about a third. In 2021 Covaxin, India's own COVID-19 vaccine, came out of Bharat Biotech's labs here. The city also has some of India's largest pharmaceutical companies, such as Dr. Reddy's and Aurobindo, and pharma is a major export.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hyderabad's second industry, bigger in global importance than most people know.
spotlights.memory_hook: A vial of Covaxin, made 30 km from the Charminar.

spotlights.name: Kaleshwaram Lift Irrigation Project

where.label: Medigadda to Kondapochamma, along the Godavari

spotlights.spot_it: Huge pump houses half-buried in hills, giant pipes, and a chain of new reservoirs that look like inland seas on satellite images.
spotlights.story_md: The Kaleshwaram project is often called the world's largest multi-stage lift irrigation scheme. Because the Godavari flows far below most of Telangana's farmland, it lifts water hundreds of metres, in stages, through barrages, pump houses, tunnels and a chain of reservoirs such as Mallanna Sagar. It was opened on 21 June 2019 at a cost of about ₹80,000 crore. In October 2023 several piers of the Medigadda barrage, the first link, sank. The national dam safety authority blamed design and construction, the auditor questioned its economics, and a judicial commission reported in 2025. It is now the centre of the state's political fight.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The biggest bet of the new state, and its biggest controversy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A river pushed uphill, until the first barrage sank.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Telangana's past is full of good stories, and guides tell them as facts. Some are true, some are half true, and some are legends that historians cannot confirm. The rule of thumb: if a story is about a clever king, a lover, a miracle or an echo, ask who wrote it down and when.

The table sorts the common claims. The most serious one is about 1948. Indian textbooks long called Operation Polo a short, almost bloodless police action. For the army it was. For civilians in the countryside, especially Muslims after the Razakars collapsed, it was not, and the government's own inquiry kept its numbers secret for 65 years.

data.Claim: Hyderabad was named Bhagyanagar after the sultan's lover Bhagmati
data.Verdict: Legend. No contemporary record of her; the name may come from bhagya, fortune, or from gardens.

data.Claim: A clap at Golconda's gate is heard at the summit, as an alarm
data.Verdict: The echo is real; its use as an alarm is a guide's story.

data.Claim: Ramappa's tower bricks float on water
data.Verdict: Light porous bricks are reported; floating is claimed, not documented by a published test.

data.Claim: The Thousand Pillar Temple has 1,000 pillars
data.Verdict: A figure of speech for very many.
For the army, nearly. Civilian deaths were estimated at 30,000 to 40,000 by the Sunderlal Committee.

data.Claim: Telangana Telugu is a corrupt form of the standard
data.Verdict: False. It is a regional variety; the standard is a social choice.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
As of October 2026 the Congress government of A. Revanth Reddy, in office since December 2023, is building its own monuments and prosecuting its predecessor's. A judicial commission under Justice P. C. Ghose reported in July 2025 that the Kaleshwaram barrages were badly planned and built, and in September 2025 the state handed the case to the CBI; the former Chief Minister K. Chandrashekar Rao is challenging it in court.

Its own big bets are a 55 km Musi riverfront through Hyderabad, with a first phase of about ₹6,500 to 7,000 crore announced in March 2026, a 30,000-acre Bharat Future City south-east of the city, the takeover of the Hyderabad Metro from L&T for about ₹15,000 crore, and a Telangana Rising 2047 plan that aims at a US$3 trillion economy. A 42% quota for Backward Classes in local bodies was stayed by the High Court in October 2025.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
1. A landlocked Deccan plateau of ancient granite, thin rain and about 46,000 tanks, with the Godavari in the north and the Krishna in the south.
2. The Kakatiyas of Warangal (1163 to 1323) left tanks, star-shaped temples such as Ramappa, and a woman king, Rudrama Devi.
3. The Qutb Shahis built Golconda's wealth on diamonds and founded Hyderabad in 1591 around the Charminar; the Nizams ruled from 1724 to 1948 and built the modern city.
4. A peasant revolt (1946), Operation Polo (1948), the 1956 merger, and a 60-year movement led to statehood on 2 June 2014.
5. Recognise on sight: a Bathukamma flower tower, a Bonalu pot, Gusadi's peacock crown, Cheriyal's red-ground scrolls, Pochampally ikat, lac bangles, dum biryani, haleem, sakinalu.
6. Now: Kaleshwaram is a CBI case, the Musi riverfront and Future City are the new bets, and the Metro has become state property.

best_facts.fact: The last Nizam of Hyderabad, called the richest man in the world by Time in 1937, used the 185-carat Jacob Diamond as a paperweight and was known for darning his own socks.
best_facts.why_surprising: Unimaginable wealth and extreme thrift in one man.

best_facts.fact: At the Medaram Jatara devotees offer jaggery, which they call bangaram, gold, often their own body weight in it. About 2,000 people came in 1955; in 2026 estimates ran from 80 lakh to over 1.6 crore.
best_facts.why_surprising: A forest fair grew several thousand times in 70 years.

best_facts.fact: Ramappa Temple is named after its sculptor, Ramappa, rather than its god or its patron, which is rare in Indian temple history.
best_facts.why_surprising: Artists are almost never the name on the building.

best_facts.fact: Osmania University, founded in 1918, was the first university in India to teach every subject, medicine and engineering included, in an Indian language: Urdu.
best_facts.why_surprising: Decades before anyone tried it in Hindi or Tamil.

best_facts.fact: The Koh-i-Noor and the Hope Diamond are both tied to the mines whose stones were sold at Golconda; until Brazil's finds in the 1720s, India supplied almost all the world's diamonds.
best_facts.why_surprising: Two of the world's most famous jewels share one Deccan source.

best_facts.fact: In many Telangana villages Muharram, Peerla Panduga, is kept mostly by Hindus, who raise the metal standards, sing laments and walk on fire.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Shia mourning month became a Hindu village festival.

best_facts.fact: The 18 m granite Buddha of Hussain Sagar toppled into the lake while being moved into place in 1990 and took two years to raise.
best_facts.why_surprising: A monolith sank before it was ever unveiled.

best_facts.fact: Operation Polo cost the Indian Army fewer than 10 dead in about four days, but a government inquiry estimated 30,000 to 40,000 civilian deaths in the violence around it and kept the report secret until 2013.
best_facts.why_surprising: The 'police action' of the textbooks hid a massacre-scale toll.

best_facts.fact: Lambadi was the mother tongue of 5.55% of Telangana in 2011, more than three times as many people as Hindi.
best_facts.why_surprising: A caravan traders' tongue outnumbers the national language.

best_facts.fact: Medak Cathedral, among the largest churches in Asia when built, rose as famine relief: its missionary paid hungry workers in grain from 1914 to 1924.
best_facts.why_surprising: A cathedral as a food-for-work scheme.

best_facts.fact: Rudrama Devi was raised and titled as a prince, Rudradeva, and Marco Polo described her kingdom as ruled by a wise widowed queen.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 13th-century woman ruled as a king.

best_facts.fact: Hyderabadi haleem was the first non-vegetarian dish in India to get a Geographical Indication tag, in 2010; during Ramzan about 6,000 places sell it.
best_facts.why_surprising: A GI tag usually goes to a sari or a sweet, not a meat porridge.

best_facts.fact: The Kaleshwaram project lifts Godavari water hundreds of metres uphill; four years after opening, piers of its first barrage sank, and in 2025 the state sent the case to the CBI.
best_facts.why_surprising: The state's proudest project became its biggest scandal.

best_facts.fact: Hyderabad's vaccine makers are often said to produce about a third of the world's vaccine doses.
best_facts.why_surprising: One city, a third of the planet's shots.

best_facts.fact: A Pochampally weaver, Chintakindi Mallesham, invented a machine to wind ikat yarn to spare his mother's aching arms; his story became a 2019 film.
best_facts.why_surprising: A village inventor got a biopic.

best_facts.fact: The Andhra Pradesh Assembly rejected the Telangana bill by voice vote; Parliament passed it anyway in February 2014.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state was split against its own Assembly's vote.

best_facts.fact: On 29 September 2025 a Bathukamma flower tower about 63 feet high, made from roughly seven tonnes of flowers, set a Guinness World Record.
best_facts.why_surprising: A household ritual scaled to a six-storey tower.

best_facts.fact: Telangana's per capita income rose from about ₹1.24 lakh in 2014-15 to about ₹4.19 lakh in 2025-26, nearly twice India's.
best_facts.why_surprising: The youngest state became one of the richest per person.

side_dish.title: Why Golconda had diamonds
side_dish.body_md:
Diamonds form about 150 to 200 km down, in the mantle, where pressure squeezes carbon into its densest crystal. They reach the surface only in rare, violent eruptions that punch narrow pipes of a rock called kimberlite, or the related lamproite, up through the crust in hours. Most of those pipes are hundreds of millions of years old.

In the Deccan the pipes were exposed and worn down long ago. Rain and rivers broke the rock, and diamonds, being hard and heavy, survived the trip downstream and settled in gravel beds with other heavy minerals. That is why the old Indian mines, such as Kollur on the Krishna, were not deep shafts but wide pits in river gravels, worked by thousands of labourers who washed and sorted by hand.

Alluvial diamonds have a bonus: the river has already done the quality control. Cracked stones break up on the way; the ones that survive tend to be tough, clean crystals. That helps explain why Indian stones such as the Koh-i-Noor and the blue that became the Hope were so prized.

The gravels ran out by the 18th century, just as Brazil and then South Africa took over. Kimberlite pipes have since been mapped in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, around Wajrakarur and Narayanpet, but none has become a big mine. Golconda's diamonds were a one-time gift of erosion.

offline_task.title: Make sarva pindi, Telangana's crisp rice pancake
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 2. About 30 minutes, plus 1 hour to soak the dal.**

**You need**
- 1 cup rice flour
- 2 tablespoons chana dal, soaked 1 hour and drained
- 2 tablespoons raw peanuts
- 1 teaspoon white sesame
- 1 small onion, finely chopped
- 2 green chillies, chopped; a few curry leaves; a handful of coriander
- Salt, about 3 tablespoons oil, warm water

**Do**
1. Mix the flour, dal, peanuts, sesame, onion, chillies, curry leaves, coriander and salt. Add warm water little by little to make a soft, slightly sticky dough.
2. Grease a heavy kadai or thick pan with 1 tablespoon oil, cold.
3. Put a ball of dough in the middle and press it out with wet fingers into a thin round across the base, about 5 mm thick.
4. Poke 5 or 6 holes with your finger and pour a few drops of oil into each.
5. Cover and cook on medium-low for 8 to 10 minutes, until the bottom is brown and crisp and the top is dry. Do not flip.
6. Lift out with a spatula and eat hot with curd or peanut chutney.

The finger holes are the signature: they let the steam out and the oil in. If you can find jowar flour, try half and half for a village version.
